walkthroughs.title: Persistent morning cough and exertional breathlessness

doorway: I cough up mucus every morning and get winded more easily.
Vital signs are available on the chart.
Perform a focused history and physical examination, discuss your plan, and document only what you obtain.
Use the time limit stated for your selected practice mode.

timeline.student: Hello, I am a medical student. I will listen to your concerns, examine you with your permission, and discuss the next steps.
timeline.patient: Hello. Thank you for introducing yourself. I am ready to talk.

timeline.student: What brings you in today?
timeline.patient: I cough up mucus every morning and get winded more easily.
timeline.why: Distinguish chronic airflow limitation from recurrent suppurative disease and malignancy.

timeline.student: How long have you had the cough?
timeline.patient: For about two years.
timeline.why: Has breathlessness or sputum changed suddenly, or gradually over months?

timeline.student: How has your breathing changed?
timeline.patient: Over 6 months I have gone from climbing two flights easily to stopping after one.
timeline.why: Change over time can change urgency even when the symptom is familiar.

timeline.student: Where do you feel the breathing discomfort?
timeline.patient: Across my chest when I am exerting myself.

timeline.student: What do you cough up?
timeline.patient: A few tablespoons of white mucus most mornings.
timeline.why: Use the patient’s words before translating them into a clinical description.

timeline.student: Are you breathless while resting or talking?
timeline.patient: No, I am comfortable sitting and talking.
timeline.why: Intensity and functional effect are distinct; record only the dimension answered.

timeline.student: Is the cough present every day?
timeline.patient: Most days, including through both winters and summers.
timeline.why: Separate time since onset from duration of one episode and from continuity.

timeline.student: What exposures have you had at work?
timeline.patient: I worked around diesel exhaust at a loading dock for 25 years.

timeline.student: What helps?
timeline.patient: Rest helps my breathing, and coughing clears the mucus for a while.
timeline.why: Relief changes probability, but is not proof that a serious cause is excluded.

timeline.student: What makes the cough or breathing worse?
timeline.patient: Stairs, smoke and cold mornings.
timeline.why: Compare triggers with the chronology; one trigger does not establish a diagnosis.

timeline.student: What have you tried for the cough?
timeline.patient: A cough syrup did not help. I have never used an inhaler.

timeline.student: Have you had chest infections before?
timeline.patient: I was treated for two chest infections in the past three years.

timeline.student: Have you had wheezing?
timeline.patient: Sometimes I hear a whistle when I breathe out.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Have you had sputum?
timeline.patient: The amount and white color have not changed recently.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Have you had hemoptysis?
timeline.patient: There has never been blood in the mucus.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you had a fever?
timeline.patient: I have not had fever.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you had weight loss?
timeline.patient: I have not lost weight.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you had night sweats?
timeline.patient: No drenching night sweats.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you had chest pain?
timeline.patient: No chest pain.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you had orthopnea?
timeline.patient: I lie flat without getting breathless.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you had edema?
timeline.patient: My ankles do not swell.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: What medical conditions have you been diagnosed with?
timeline.patient: High blood pressure. Nobody has diagnosed a lung condition.

timeline.student: Have you had surgery?
timeline.patient: My gallbladder was removed at 42.

timeline.student: What medicines do you take?
timeline.patient: Amlodipine 5 milligrams each morning.
timeline.why: Name, dose and frequency matter; do not fill in missing details.

timeline.student: Do you have any medication allergies?
timeline.patient: No known medicine allergies.
timeline.why: Distinguish the substance and reaction from a blanket allergy label.

timeline.student: Do you smoke?
timeline.patient: I smoked a pack a day for 32 years. I quit two years ago.

timeline.student: How much alcohol do you drink?
timeline.patient: Two beers with dinner on Friday and Saturday.

timeline.student: Do you use recreational drugs?
timeline.patient: No.

timeline.student: What do you do now for work?
timeline.patient: I drive a delivery van. Unloading boxes is getting difficult.

timeline.student: Who lives with you and can help with appointments?
timeline.patient: I live alone. My daughter can drive me, but I lose pay for weekday visits.

timeline.student: What serious illnesses run in your family?
timeline.patient: My father died of lung cancer at 68. He smoked too.
timeline.why: Record which relative and the condition; do not infer a family history from patient worry.

timeline.student: What about your mother and siblings?
timeline.patient: My mother has high blood pressure. My brother has no major illness that I know of.
timeline.why: Record which relative and the condition; do not infer a family history from patient worry.

timeline.student: What worries you about the cough?
timeline.patient: My father had lung cancer. I am afraid I have it too.

timeline.student: Thank you for explaining that. I can understand why this is concerning.
timeline.patient: Like I said, my father had lung cancer. I am afraid I have it too. Could you say that another way?

timeline.student: May I have your permission to examine you?
timeline.patient: Yes, that's fine. Go ahead.

timeline.action: Clean hands, provide privacy and appropriate draping, explain the selected examination and help the patient into a comfortable position.
timeline.why: These are stated actions in this written example. A visual avatar does not verify hand hygiene, consent or hands-on technique.

timeline.finding: Comfortable at rest, speaking full sentences.
timeline.why: Use the supported case-specific maneuvers and document their actual findings; do not infer normal findings from the generic model.

timeline.action: Auscultate heart — aortic, pulmonic, tricuspid, mitral, on skin
timeline.finding: Regular rate and rhythm without murmur.
timeline.why: The course expects at least four listening posts, on skin.

timeline.action: Auscultate lungs — posterior, on skin, compare side to side, mouth open
timeline.finding: Breath sounds mildly reduced bilaterally with prolonged expiration and scattered expiratory wheezes; no focal crackles.
timeline.why: The course expects six posterior fields, mouth open, on skin, comparing sides.

timeline.action: Inspect chest wall — symmetry, accessory muscle use
timeline.finding: Symmetric chest expansion; no accessory muscle use at rest.
timeline.why: This specific action releases only the finding shown here. Interpret it with the history; it does not confirm a diagnosis by itself.

timeline.action: Percuss lung fields — posterior, compare side to side
timeline.finding: Mildly increased resonance symmetrically over posterior fields.
timeline.why: This specific action releases only the finding shown here. Interpret it with the history; it does not confirm a diagnosis by itself.

timeline.action: Inspect / palpate extremities — edema, clubbing, cyanosis
timeline.finding: No peripheral edema, digital clubbing or cyanosis.
timeline.why: This specific action releases only the finding shown here. Interpret it with the history; it does not confirm a diagnosis by itself.

timeline.finding: T4 bilateral thoracic paraspinal tissue texture change and tenderness.
timeline.why: Name the level examined; findings are released by region.

timeline.student: I will arrange breathing tests and a chest image rather than assuming the cough is just from past smoking. We will review the results in two weeks. Sudden severe breathing trouble or coughing blood needs earlier help.
timeline.patient: Thank you. I understand that the next steps depend on the examination and tests.
timeline.why: Proposed care, not a record of tests or treatment already completed.

timeline.student: What questions do you have about the next steps?
timeline.patient: My father had lung cancer. I am afraid I have it too.

timeline.student: We can look for an appointment that limits lost work time and coordinate transport with your daughter if you wish.
timeline.patient: That would help. Thank you.
timeline.why: Answer the concern that was just expressed. Give a defensible recommendation and explain uncertainty; do not promise a diagnosis or recovery before the evidence supports it.

note.S:
CC: I cough up mucus every morning and get winded more easily.

HPI: 56-year-old male. Productive cough for 2 years. Several tablespoons of white morning sputum. Symptoms most days year-round. Progressive exertional dyspnea over 6 months; now stops after one flight. No resting or conversational dyspnea. Diffuse exertional breathing discomfort. 25 years of loading-dock diesel exposure. Worse with exertion, smoke and cold air. Rest relieves dyspnea; expectoration temporarily clears mucus. Cough syrup ineffective; no inhaler use. Two treated chest infections in 3 years.

PMH: Hypertension; no established lung diagnosis.

PSH: Cholecystectomy at 42.

Meds: Amlodipine 5 mg daily.

SH: Former smoker: 32 pack-years, quit 2 years ago. Four beers weekly. No recreational drugs. Delivery driver; limited during unloading. Lives alone; daughter can transport; visits cause lost pay.

FH: Father: lung cancer at 68; father smoked. Mother: hypertension; brother: no known major illness.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

ROS: Respiratory: Intermittent expiratory wheeze. No hemoptysis. No recent sputum volume or color change. General: No fever. No weight loss. No night sweats. Cardiovascular: No chest pain. No orthopnea. No edema.
note.O:
Vitals: BP 132/80 mmHg, P 82 bpm, R 18 rpm, T 98.1 F oral, Pulse Ox 95% on room air, Ht 5' 9", Wt 178 lbs

General: Comfortable at rest, speaking full sentences.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm without murmur.
Lungs: Breath sounds mildly reduced bilaterally with prolonged expiration and scattered expiratory wheezes; no focal crackles.
Lungs: Symmetric chest expansion; no accessory muscle use at rest.
Lungs: Mildly increased resonance symmetrically over posterior fields.
Extremities: No peripheral edema, digital clubbing or cyanosis.
Osteopathic: T4 bilateral thoracic paraspinal tissue texture change and tenderness.
P: 1. Obtain post-bronchodilator spirometry and chest radiograph; assess symptoms and exacerbation history. If COPD is confirmed, select inhaled bronchodilator therapy and teach technique; review vaccination and continued smoking abstinence. Arrange review in 2 weeks around work. Acute breathlessness, confusion or blue lips needs emergency care.

2. If sputum/infection history or initial imaging remains concerning, arrange thin-section chest CT and sputum studies when indicated; respiratory referral can guide airway clearance. Explain infection warning signs and avoid empiric long-term antibiotics.
3. Investigate persistent cough with diagnostic chest imaging and escalate suspicious findings to a lung specialist promptly. Discuss that risk is not a diagnosis and reinforce smoking abstinence.

walkthroughs.estimate_method: 150 spoken words/minute plus the full simulation examination durations and 55 seconds for introductions and transitions; explanatory commentary excluded. This is a planning estimate, not a measured student performance.

reasoning.question: Has breathlessness or sputum changed suddenly, or gradually over months?
reasoning.why: Distinguish chronic airflow limitation from recurrent suppurative disease and malignancy.
reasoning.if_present: Use the reported pattern to select the relevant examinations and assess urgency.
reasoning.if_absent: Keep alternatives open and ask a focused follow-up.
reasoning.document: Separate reported symptoms, observed signs, assessment and proposed care.

differentials.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
differentials.teaching_context: Chronic productive cough, progressive exertional dyspnea and smoke exposure support COPD; spirometry is needed.

differentials.name: Bronchiectasis
differentials.teaching_context: Daily sputum and recurrent infections support this alternative; imaging is required and infection history is not proof of cause.

differentials.name: Lung malignancy
differentials.teaching_context: Persistent symptoms, age and smoking exposure warrant exclusion despite no hemoptysis or weight loss.

omissions: Explaining uncertainty and the practical follow-up plan.
